display.text: For independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance, the standardized sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows. Here it explains approximate normality of large-sample Bernoulli proportions. Abbreviated CLT.

Adjusting integer count boundaries by half a unit when approximating a discrete binomial probability with a continuous normal distribution; for example, X ≤ k is approximated using a normal cutoff k + 0.5.
A distribution cutoff corresponding to a chosen tail probability; the R exercise obtains a standard normal cutoff with 5% of probability above it.
The probability that a variable falls below a specified value, represented by the density area to that value's left.
A distribution's halfway point, with half its probability on each side in the continuous case. For a normal distribution, the median equals the mean.
A cutoff indicating a specified percentage of values below it; the kth percentile of a continuous distribution has k% of its probability below that value.
Cutoffs dividing a distribution into four equal probability portions. Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q2 the median, and Q3 the 75th percentile.
The probability that a variable exceeds a specified value. For a continuous distribution it equals 1 minus the left-tail probability at that value.
For a normal distribution, approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, respectively. Also called 68–95–99.7 rule.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, obtained as Z = (X − μ)/σ when X is normal.
Converting a value to z = (x − μ)/σ to express its position relative to its distribution. Standardizing a normal variable produces a standard normal variable.
The matching shape on either side of the mean, giving equal probabilities to equally distant corresponding intervals; in particular, P(Z > z) = P(Z < −z).
Converting a z-score back to the original measurement scale using x = μ + zσ.
A value's signed distance from its mean in standard-deviation units: z = (x − μ)/σ. Positive values are above the mean, negative values below it. Also called standardized value.
